title: A Signal in the Sky
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 10 of 40
content:
The Prydwen arrived at dusk.

At first I thought the sky was burning.

A deep mechanical thunder rolled across Cambridge, too steady for weather and too vast for any machine I knew. Dust shook from the police station ceiling. Rhys came out of his chair with his rifle already raised. Haylen ran for the door.

Danse was outside before all of us.

I followed him into the street.

The airship emerged above the ruined skyline like a piece of another world.

It was enormous.

A steel fortress suspended beneath gas cells, engines roaring, spotlights sweeping across rooftops. Vertibirds circled it in formation. Brotherhood insignia marked the hull.

For once, I had nothing sarcastic to say.

Danse stood in the middle of the street with his face tilted upward.

The expression on him was so open that I almost felt like I was intruding.

Pride.

Relief.

Home.

“There,” he said softly.

I moved beside him.

“You weren’t exaggerating.”

“I rarely exaggerate.”

“I’m learning that.”

The Prydwen passed overhead, blotting out the evening light.

Wind from the engines sent trash spinning across the street.

Haylen was laughing.

Rhys looked as if someone had handed him the Commonwealth and apologized for the delay.

Danse simply watched.

Then a transmission crackled over his radio.

His entire posture changed.

“Paladin Danse, Recon Squad Gladius. Receiving.”

The voice on the other end ordered the surviving squad to report for reassignment and instructed Danse to prepare a recruit for transport if appropriate.

His eyes moved to me.

I knew immediately what recruit meant.

After the message ended, Haylen squeezed my shoulder.

“Looks like you’re getting the grand tour.”

“I haven’t agreed to anything.”

Rhys snorted.

Danse ignored him.

“No,” he said. “You haven’t.”

The others went inside to prepare.

Danse stayed with me in the street.

The airship’s shadow moved over the buildings.

“You can say no,” he said.

“That sounded painful.”

“I’m serious.”

“I know.”

He looked toward the Prydwen.

“The Brotherhood can offer training, equipment, resources. But joining means accepting a chain of command. It means obligations. I won’t misrepresent that.”

“And the speeches about humanity?”

“Those are included.”

I laughed.

He did not quite smile.

“Do you want me to join?”

The question surprised him.

Danse looked at me for several seconds.

“As your commanding officer, I think you would be an asset.”

“You’re not my commanding officer yet.”

His jaw tightened.

“As your…”

He stopped.

Friend, I thought.

He had used the word once. He still treated it like something breakable.

“As someone whose opinion you apparently value,” he said finally, “yes. I want you there.”

My chest did something inconvenient.

“Why?”

“You’re capable.”

“Danse.”

“You’re reliable.”

“Danse.”

“You ask too many questions.”

“That sounds like a negative.”

“It can be.”

He exhaled.

Then, quieter, “You make this place easier.”

The Commonwealth had trained me to expect affection disguised as barter, threats disguised as jokes, loneliness disguised as independence.

Danse disguised almost everything as logistics.

I understood him anyway.

“I’ll go,” I said.

His shoulders relaxed.

“Good.”

“Not outstanding?”

The smile appeared.

“Don’t push your luck.”

The vertibird arrived an hour later.

I had ridden in one exactly never times.

Danse climbed aboard like the machine was an extension of the floor. I climbed aboard like a person reconsidering several life choices.

He noticed immediately.

“You’re fine.”

“I’m sitting in an open-sided aircraft held together by rotors and optimism.”

“Vertibirds are reliable.”

“You say that like you didn’t tell me everything made before the war is dangerous.”

“This model is maintained by Brotherhood technicians.”

“Ah. So dangerous with paperwork.”

The aircraft lifted.

My stomach stayed in Cambridge.

I grabbed the nearest stable object.

It turned out to be Danse’s forearm.

He looked down at my hand.

I looked down too.

“Sorry.”

“You can hold on.”

“I’m fine.”

The vertibird banked.

I held on harder.

Danse’s mouth twitched.

“Not a word.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You were going to.”

“I notice patterns.”

I glared at him.

He had the decency to look pleased.

Boston spread beneath us in broken towers and dark streets. The Prydwen grew larger until it stopped looking like a ship and became architecture.

We landed on the flight deck among soldiers, crates, cables, and the constant noise of engines.

Danse stepped down first.

Then he turned and offered me his hand.

Not because I needed help.

Because he wanted to.

I knew the difference.

I took it.

His grip was firm and warm, callused across the palm. He steadied me as the deck vibrated beneath our feet.

For a second neither of us let go.

Then someone shouted, “Paladin Danse!”

He released me immediately.

Command returned to his spine.

“Stay close,” he said.

I looked up at the massive interior of the airship, the Brotherhood banners, the soldiers moving with practiced urgency.

“You worried I’ll get lost?”

“No.”

He looked at me, dark eyes serious beneath the deck lights.

“I’m worried they’ll decide you belong somewhere else.”

The admission was so unexpected that I forgot to breathe.

Danse seemed to realize what he had said.

His expression tightened.

“Come on. Elder Maxson is waiting.”

He turned before I could answer.

I followed him into the Prydwen.

Behind us, the Commonwealth disappeared beneath steel.

The flight up was louder than fear and somehow not loud enough to drown it.

I had ridden vertibirds before only in the loosest sense of the word *ridden*: once hanging onto a landing strut while someone shot at me, which I did not count as transportation so much as a prolonged mistake.

This time Danse strapped me in himself.

“I know how buckles work.”

“I’m verifying the harness.”

“You checked it twice.”

“I’m verifying it a third time.”

“Is three a Brotherhood regulation?”

“No.”

“Then you’re nervous.”

His hands stopped at the clasp across my chest.

“I am not nervous about the flight.”

“Interesting qualifier.”

The engines rose before he could answer.

Cambridge dropped beneath us. The city became a map of ruined blocks and green-gray river water. Then the Prydwen filled the sky ahead—larger with every second, armored belly suspended beneath its vast gas envelope, vertibirds circling like insects around an impossible animal.

Danse watched it with something I had not seen on his face before.

Relief.

Not simple pride. Not worship.

Homecoming.

“These are your people,” I said.

“Yes.”

The word came softer than usual.

“You thought they weren’t coming.”

Danse looked at me.

For weeks he had behaved as though confidence could substitute for certainty. Standing in the vertibird with the airship growing before us, he finally let the truth exist.

“We lost contact with the Citadel before entering the Commonwealth. After what happened to the squad…”

He stopped.

“I considered the possibility that our distress calls would never be received.”

“And now?”

“Now we report.”

Of course.

Feel something, turn it into a task.

I reached across the narrow space between our seats and touched the back of his glove.

His eyes dropped to the contact.

I almost moved away.

Then his hand turned under mine.

Not enough to hold it. Enough that our palms met through leather.

The vertibird banked.

Danse’s other hand shot to my harness on reflex.

“I’m strapped in.”

“I know.”

His grip remained.

Below us, the Commonwealth stretched all the way to the horizon—every settlement, ruin, ghoul, raider, farm, synth, and person the Brotherhood had come here to judge and protect and command.

I wondered which parts of Danse had been shaped by the organization waiting above us and which parts had survived it.

He seemed to sense the direction of my thoughts.

“When we board, there will be procedures.”

“Of course there will.”

“You’ll be questioned.”

“Do I get to question them back?”

“No.”

“Seems unfair.”

The Prydwen filled the forward opening of the vertibird until I could make out people moving on the flight deck.

Danse checked the straps on my harness for the second time.

“They were secure the first time.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you checking?”

“Turbulence.”

“There isn’t any.”

“There could be.”

I stared at him.

He stared back with the solemn dignity of a man who had been caught worrying and intended to classify the emotion as preventative maintenance.

“What happens when we land?” I asked.

“You’ll be processed as a civilian auxiliary until Maxson determines your status.”

“That sounds flattering.”

“It means don’t wander into restricted areas.”

“I never wander.”

“You wandered into a Brotherhood firefight.”

“That was purposeful curiosity.”

“That is not better.”

The corner of his mouth moved.

For all his pride in the ship, he was nervous about bringing me aboard. I could hear it in the extra instructions, see it in the way his eyes kept returning to me whenever another squad crossed the deck below.

Cambridge had been his problem.

The Prydwen was his world.

Apparently introducing me to it required a briefing.

“Try not to antagonize anyone of superior rank.”

“How many people on that ship outrank me?”

“All of them.”

“That gives me tremendous freedom.”

Danse closed his eyes briefly.

“I am already reconsidering this.”

“No, you’re not.”

His gaze returned to me.

The vertibird shuddered in the Prydwen’s wake.

“No,” he admitted. “I’m not.”

The landing deck rushed toward us.

Danse finally withdrew his hand to check his weapon and square his shoulders.

By the time the skids hit metal, Paladin Danse was back in place: spine straight, expression controlled, ready to present himself to the Brotherhood as though Cambridge had never frightened him.

But I had seen the moment before the armor settled.

I carried it with me when the side door opened.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
